content: Diabetes mellitus (DM) encompasses a group of metabolic disorders characterized by hyperglycemia, which arises due to various underlying mechanisms. These mechanisms include reduced insulin secretion, insulin resistance, impaired glucose utilization, and increased glucose production. Hyperglycemia, in turn, can lead to secondary metabolic disturbances affecting multiple organ systems. DM is a major global health concern and is the leading cause of end-stage renal disease (ESRD), non-traumatic lower extremity amputations, and adult blindness. Early diagnosis and treatment are critical to reducing the associated morbidity and mortality. The prevalence of diabetes is increasing worldwide, with the World Health Organization (WHO) reporting that 346 million people were affected as of recent estimates, a number expected to double by 2030. While diabetes is more prevalent in developed countries, complications leading to death are more common in developing nations. Type 2 diabetes is significantly more common than type 1 diabetes. Diabetes can result in both acute and chronic complications. Acute complications include hypoglycemia, diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), and hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (HHS). Chronic complications are categorized as macrovascular (e.g., coronary heart disease, peripheral arterial disease, cerebrovascular disease), microvascular (e.g., retinopathy, neuropathy, nephropathy), and other organ-specific complications (e.g., gastrointestinal, genitourinary, dermatologic, infectious, ocular, periodontal, and auditory issues). The primary goals of diabetes management are to alleviate hyperglycemic symptoms, prevent long-term complications, and improve the patient’s quality of life. Classification of Diabetes Mellitus Diabetes mellitus is classified into three main types based on the underlying pathogenic mechanisms: 1. Type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM): Characterized by autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells, leading to absolute insulin deficiency. 2. Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM): Associated with insulin resistance and relative insulin deficiency. 3. Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM): Hyperglycemia first recognized during pregnancy. Complications of Diabetes Mellitus Acute Complications: Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA): Commonly seen in type 1 diabetes but can also occur in type 2 diabetes. It is often the initial presentation of type 1 diabetes. Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (HHS): More frequently observed in elderly patients with type 2 diabetes. Chronic Complications: 1. Macrovascular Complications: Coronary heart disease Peripheral arterial disease Cerebrovascular disease 2. Microvascular Complications: Retinopathy (nonproliferative and proliferative forms) Macular edema Neuropathy (sensory, motor, and autonomic) Nephropathy (albuminuria and progressive renal dysfunction) 3. Other Organ-Specific Complications: Gastrointestinal (e.g., gastroparesis, diarrhea) Genitourinary (e.g., uropathy, sexual dysfunction) Dermatologic conditions Increased susceptibility to infections Ocular issues (e.g., cataracts, glaucoma) Periodontal disease Hearing loss Gestational diabetes has unique complications for both the mother and fetus, including pregnancy-specific risks and developmental concerns. Diagnosis of Diabetes Mellitus Diagnostic Criteria for Type 1 and Type 2 Diabetes: Symptoms of diabetes plus a random plasma glucose concentration ≥200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L). Fasting plasma glucose (FPG) ≥126 mg/dL (7.0 mmol/L) after no caloric intake for at least 8 hours. Hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) ≥6.5%. Plasma glucose ≥200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) 2 hours after a 75-g oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT). The HbA1c test should be performed using a method certified by the National Glycohemoglobin Standardization Program (NGSP) and standardized to the Diabetes Control and Complications Trial (DCCT) assay. Conditions such as hemoglobinopathies, increased red blood cell turnover, or recent blood transfusions may interfere with HbA1c results, necessitating reliance on plasma glucose criteria for diagnosis. Diagnostic Criteria for Gestational Diabetes: One-Step Strategy: A 75-g OGTT performed at 24–28 weeks of gestation. Diagnosis is made if any of the following thresholds are met: Fasting glucose ≥92 mg/dL (5.1 mmol/L) 1-hour glucose ≥180 mg/dL (10.0 mmol/L) 2-hour glucose ≥153 mg/dL (8.5 mmol/L) Two-Step Strategy: A 50-g glucose load test (non-fasting) followed by a 100-g OGTT for those with positive screening results. Diagnosis requires at least two abnormal values during the 100-g OGTT. Screening Recommendations Type 1 Diabetes: Routine screening for type 1 diabetes is not recommended. Type 2 Diabetes: Screening is recommended for individuals with risk factors, including: Overweight or obesity (BMI >25 kg/m² or >23 kg/m² in Asian Americans) with additional risk factors. All individuals aged 45 years or older. Children and adolescents who are overweight or obese with additional risk factors. Gestational Diabetes: All pregnant women should be screened for gestational diabetes between 24–28 weeks of gestation using a 50-g glucose test. High-risk women (e.g., those with a family history of diabetes, obesity, or prior gestational diabetes) should be screened at the first prenatal visit. Prevention of Diabetes Mellitus Lifestyle modification is the cornerstone of diabetes prevention. This includes dietary changes, weight reduction, and regular physical activity. The Diabetes Prevention Program (DPP) demonstrated that intensive lifestyle interventions could reduce the incidence of type 2 diabetes by 58% over three years. Key components of lifestyle modification include: Increased physical activity Weight loss Reduced intake of saturated fats Increased dietary fiber consumption Behavioral interventions to maintain adherence Pharmacologic interventions, such as the use of acarbose, have also shown promise in preventing diabetes in individuals with impaired glucose tolerance. However, lifestyle changes remain the most effective and sustainable approach to diabetes prevention.
